meta.title: Advanced English Grammar – Multi-Error Test (B2–C2)
meta.description: Identify and correct grammatical errors in advanced sentences. Each item combines at least two advanced grammar topics. Some sentences contain more than one error.

questions.question: The sentence may contain 0, 1 or multiple errors. Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form. If no error, choose No Error.

details_explanation.explanation: The sentence uses an inverted third conditional. The if-clause refers to the past, so the main clause must also refer to the past with would have + past participle.
details_explanation.introduction: Inverted conditionals omit if and place had, should or were before the subject. The main clause must match the time frame established by the if-clause.

rules.title: 1. Inversion with had
rules.explanation: In a third conditional, if + had + past participle can become Had + subject + past participle.
rules.structure: Had + subject + past participle, subject + would have + past participle.
notes: No if is used.
The main clause keeps would have.

rules.title: 2. Mixed conditionals
rules.explanation: When the if-clause is past and the result is also past, use would have + past participle.
rules.structure: If + past perfect, subject + would have + past participle.
notes: Do not use would + base form for a past result.

common_mistakes.wrong: Had I known, I would not approve the plan.
common_mistakes.correct: Had I known, I would not have approved the plan.
common_mistakes.reason: The result is in the past, so the conditional perfect is required.

other_examples.sentence: Had the warning been heeded, the accident would have been prevented.
other_examples.translation: Seandainya peringatan itu diindahkan, kecelakaan itu bisa dicegah.

other_examples.sentence: Had she applied earlier, she would have been offered the position.
other_examples.translation: Seandainya dia melamar lebih awal, dia akan ditawari posisi itu.

questions.question: The sentence may contain 0, 1 or multiple errors. Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form. If no error, choose No Error.

details_explanation.explanation: The sentence combines subject-auxiliary inversion after not only with the mandative subjunctive after essential. Not only requires inversion in the first clause, and essential that requires the base form be.
details_explanation.introduction: Negative and restrictive adverbials at the beginning of a clause trigger inversion. Mandative adjectives such as essential, imperative and vital trigger the base subjunctive in the following that-clause.

rules.title: 1. Inversion after not only
rules.explanation: When not only begins a clause, the auxiliary comes before the subject.
rules.structure: Not only + auxiliary + subject + main verb ... but + subject + also + verb.
notes: The inversion applies only to the first clause.
Do not invert the but-clause.

rules.title: 2. Mandative subjunctive
rules.explanation: After adjectives such as essential, the that-clause uses the base form of the verb for all subjects.
rules.structure: It is essential + that + subject + base verb.
notes: Be is used even with he, she and it.
In informal British English, should + base verb is also possible.

common_mistakes.wrong: Not only it is essential that he is informed.
common_mistakes.correct: Not only is it essential that he be informed.
common_mistakes.reason: Not only triggers inversion, and essential that requires the base subjunctive.

other_examples.sentence: Not only did she refuse the offer, but she also criticized it publicly.
other_examples.translation: Tidak hanya dia menolak tawaran itu, tetapi dia juga mengkritiknya secara terbuka.

other_examples.sentence: It is vital that every member be present at the hearing.
other_examples.translation: Sangat penting bahwa setiap anggota hadir di sidang.

questions.question: The sentence may contain 0, 1 or multiple errors. Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form. If no error, choose No Error.

details_explanation.explanation: The sentence is an it-cleft. The relative pronoun who refers to the plural noun shareholders, so the verb must be plural: decide. The phrase not the board does not change the agreement.
details_explanation.introduction: Cleft sentences split information into two clauses for emphasis. The verb in the relative clause agrees with the focused noun, not with the singular dummy it.

rules.title: 1. It-clefts
rules.explanation: An it-cleft has the pattern It is/was + focus + relative clause.
rules.structure: It is + noun phrase + who/that + verb + rest.
notes: Who is used for people; that is also possible.
The verb agrees with the focused noun phrase.

rules.title: 2. Agreement with alternative subjects
rules.explanation: When the subject is X, not Y, the verb agrees with X.
rules.structure: X, not Y, + plural/singular verb.
notes: The not-phrase is parenthetical.
Do not let the nearer noun control agreement.

common_mistakes.wrong: It is the shareholders who decides the outcome.
common_mistakes.correct: It is the shareholders who decide the outcome.
common_mistakes.reason: The relative clause agrees with the plural shareholders.

other_examples.sentence: It is the teachers, not the parents, who are responsible for attendance.
other_examples.translation: Guru, bukan orang tua, yang bertanggung jawab atas kehadiran.

other_examples.sentence: It was the directors who approved the merger.
other_examples.translation: Para direkturlah yang menyetujui merger itu.

multiErrorSegments.text: the paintings impressed the visitors enormously
correctAnswers: the visitors were enormously impressed by the paintings
the visitors were greatly impressed by the paintings

details_explanation.explanation: The participial phrase Walking through the museum must describe the subject of the main clause. The original subject the paintings cannot walk, so the sentence contains a dangling modifier. The main clause should be passive with the visitors as the subject.
details_explanation.introduction: A participial phrase at the beginning of a sentence normally describes the subject of the main clause. If it does not, the modifier is said to dangle.

rules.title: 1. Dangling participles
rules.explanation: The understood subject of an initial participle must be the same as the subject of the main clause.
rules.structure: Participle phrase, + subject + verb + rest.
notes: Check who performs the action in the participle.
If the subject is wrong, rewrite the main clause.

rules.title: 2. Passive voice
rules.explanation: When the focus is on the experiencer rather than the agent, use the passive.
rules.structure: Subject + be + past participle + by + agent.
notes: The passive is common with impress, astonish and shock.
Keep the adverb before the past participle.

common_mistakes.wrong: Walking through the museum, the paintings impressed the visitors.
common_mistakes.correct: Walking through the museum, the visitors were impressed by the paintings.
common_mistakes.reason: The visitors, not the paintings, are walking through the museum.

other_examples.sentence: Having read the report, the committee rejected the proposal.
other_examples.translation: Setelah membaca laporan itu, komite menolak proposal tersebut.

other_examples.sentence: Shocked by the news, she could not speak.
other_examples.translation: Terkejut oleh berita itu, dia tidak bisa berbicara.

multiErrorSegments.text: No sooner the meeting had begun
correctAnswers: No sooner had the meeting begun

details_explanation.explanation: No sooner at the beginning of a clause triggers inversion: had + subject + past participle. It is also followed by than, not when. The participial phrase forcing everyone to evacuate correctly describes the result.
details_explanation.introduction: No sooner ... than is a fixed correlative structure used to show that one event happened immediately after another. It requires inversion in the first clause.

rules.title: 1. Inversion after no sooner
rules.explanation: Place the auxiliary had before the subject.
rules.structure: No sooner + had + subject + past participle + than + past simple.
notes: The first clause uses the past perfect.
The second clause uses the past simple.

rules.title: 2. Than, not when
rules.explanation: The correct second element of the correlative is than.
rules.structure: No sooner ... than ...
notes: When is used with hardly ... when and scarcely ... when.
Do not mix the two patterns.

common_mistakes.wrong: No sooner the meeting had begun when the alarm went off.
common_mistakes.correct: No sooner had the meeting begun than the alarm went off.
common_mistakes.reason: No sooner requires inversion and is followed by than.

other_examples.sentence: No sooner had she sat down than the phone rang.
other_examples.translation: Belum sempat dia duduk, telepon berdering.

other_examples.sentence: No sooner had the announcement been made than the shares fell.
other_examples.translation: Begitu pengumuman dibuat, saham langsung jatuh.

correctAnswers: Such was the intensity of the debate

details_explanation.explanation: Such is used before a noun phrase, while so is used before an adjective. Since intense is an adjective, the correct structure is So intense was the debate. Alternatively, Such was the intensity of the debate uses such before a noun phrase.
details_explanation.introduction: So and such can be fronted for emphasis, triggering inversion. So precedes an adjective or adverb; such precedes a noun phrase.

rules.title: 1. So + adjective + inversion
rules.explanation: Front so + adjective and invert the subject and verb.
rules.structure: So + adjective + be + subject + that + result clause.
notes: Use so with adjectives such as intense, clear and rapid.
The result clause is introduced by that.

rules.title: 2. Such + noun phrase
rules.explanation: Such is used before a noun phrase, often with be inversion.
rules.structure: Such + be + noun phrase + that + result clause.
notes: Such cannot directly modify an adjective.
Such a + adjective + noun is also possible.

common_mistakes.wrong: Such intense was the debate that everyone lost composure.
common_mistakes.correct: So intense was the debate that everyone lost composure.
common_mistakes.reason: Intense is an adjective, so so is required.

other_examples.sentence: So rapid was the decline that investors panicked.
other_examples.translation: Begitu cepat penurunannya sehingga para investor panik.

other_examples.sentence: Such was her influence that few dared to object.
other_examples.translation: Begitu besar pengaruhnya sehingga sedikit yang berani membantah.

details_explanation.explanation: Had it not been for introduces an unreal past condition, so the result must be would have + past participle. The phrase before an agreement was reached confirms the past time frame.
details_explanation.introduction: Had it not been for + noun phrase is an inverted alternative to If it had not been for. It describes an unreal past cause.

rules.title: 1. Had it not been for
rules.explanation: This structure replaces if it had not been for in formal English.
rules.structure: Had it not been for + noun phrase, subject + would have + past participle.
notes: It refers to an unreal past situation.
The main clause uses the conditional perfect.

rules.title: 2. Conditional perfect
rules.explanation: Use would have + past participle for an unreal past result.
rules.structure: Subject + would have + past participle.
notes: Do not use would + base form with a past result.
This applies to both if-clauses and inverted clauses.

common_mistakes.wrong: Had it not been for her help, I would fail.
common_mistakes.correct: Had it not been for her help, I would have failed.
common_mistakes.reason: The situation is in the past, so the conditional perfect is needed.

other_examples.sentence: Had it not been for the delay, we would have arrived on time.
other_examples.translation: Seandainya bukan karena keterlambatan, kami akan tiba tepat waktu.

other_examples.sentence: Had it not been for his evidence, the case would have collapsed.
other_examples.translation: Seandainya bukan karena kesaksiannya, kasus itu akan runtuh.

multiErrorSegments.text: which was submitted by the consultant
requires that every department is audited
correctAnswers: requires that every department be audited
requires every department to be audited

details_explanation.explanation: The verb require triggers the mandative subjunctive in the that-clause: every department be audited. The non-defining relative clause which was submitted by the consultant is correctly formed and passive.
details_explanation.introduction: Verbs such as require, demand, insist and recommend can be followed by that + subject + base verb. This is the mandative subjunctive, common in formal English.

rules.title: 1. Mandative subjunctive after require
rules.explanation: Use the base form of the verb in the that-clause, even with singular subjects.
rules.structure: require + that + subject + base verb.
notes: Be is used for all persons.
An alternative is require + object + to be + past participle.

rules.title: 2. Non-defining relative clauses
rules.explanation: Non-defining relative clauses add extra information and are separated by commas.
rules.structure: Noun phrase, + which/who + clause, + main verb.
notes: They cannot be reduced to a participle if the meaning would change.
The relative pronoun cannot be omitted.

common_mistakes.wrong: The rules require that every employee is trained.
common_mistakes.correct: The rules require that every employee be trained.
common_mistakes.reason: Require that takes the base subjunctive.

other_examples.sentence: The regulations require that all visitors be registered.
other_examples.translation: Peraturan mengharuskan semua pengunjung terdaftar.

other_examples.sentence: She insisted that the meeting be postponed.
other_examples.translation: Dia bersikeras agar rapat ditunda.

details_explanation.explanation: Little at the beginning of a clause is negative and triggers inversion with do-support: Little did the researchers realize. The passive would later be challenged is correctly formed with modal + be + past participle.
details_explanation.introduction: Negative adverbials such as little, rarely, seldom and never at the start of a clause require subject-auxiliary inversion.

rules.title: 1. Negative inversion with little
rules.explanation: Place the auxiliary before the subject after little.
rules.structure: Little + auxiliary + subject + main verb.
notes: Use do/does/did when there is no auxiliary.
The meaning is emphatic.

rules.title: 2. Modal passive
rules.explanation: The passive with a modal has the pattern modal + be + past participle.
rules.structure: subject + modal + be + past participle.
notes: Would later be challenged is correct.
Do not use would later be challenging for a passive meaning.

common_mistakes.wrong: Little the researchers realized the importance of the discovery.
common_mistakes.correct: Little did the researchers realize the importance of the discovery.
common_mistakes.reason: Little at the beginning requires inversion.

other_examples.sentence: Little did she suspect that she was being watched.
other_examples.translation: Sedikit pun dia tidak menduga bahwa dia sedang diawasi.

other_examples.sentence: Rarely has such a claim been made.
other_examples.translation: Jarang sekali klaim seperti itu dibuat.

correctAnswers: for the report to be submitted

multiErrorSegments.text: otherwise the grant will be revoked

details_explanation.explanation: Imperative that requires the base subjunctive: that the report be submitted. Otherwise functions as a conditional connector meaning if not, and the passive will be revoked is correct.
details_explanation.introduction: The mandative subjunctive is used after adjectives such as imperative, essential and vital. Otherwise introduces a consequence of not doing something.

rules.title: 1. Subjunctive after imperative
rules.explanation: Use the base form be in the that-clause.
rules.structure: It is imperative + that + subject + be + past participle.
notes: An infinitive alternative is for + object + to be + past participle.
The indicative is is not used in formal writing.

rules.title: 2. Otherwise as a conditional
rules.explanation: Otherwise means if not or or else and introduces the consequence.
rules.structure: Clause + otherwise + clause.
notes: It can join two independent clauses.
A comma usually precedes otherwise.

common_mistakes.wrong: It is imperative that the form is signed.
common_mistakes.correct: It is imperative that the form be signed.
common_mistakes.reason: Imperative that takes the base subjunctive.

other_examples.sentence: It is essential that all documents be verified before release.
other_examples.translation: Sangat penting bahwa semua dokumen diverifikasi sebelum dirilis.

other_examples.sentence: You must submit the form today; otherwise your application will be rejected.
other_examples.translation: Anda harus menyerahkan formulir hari ini; jika tidak, lamaran Anda akan ditolak.

questions.question: The sentence may contain 0, 1 or multiple errors. Click the incorrect parts and type the correct form. If no error, choose No Error.

multiErrorSegments.text: a candidate whose command of syntax

details_explanation.explanation: Rarely at the beginning of a clause triggers inversion: Rarely have I encountered. The comparative as impressive as hers and the possessive relative clause whose command of syntax are correct.
details_explanation.introduction: Rarely, seldom and hardly are negative adverbials that require inversion when fronted. Comparative as ... as shows equality.

rules.title: 1. Inversion after rarely
rules.explanation: Move the auxiliary before the subject.
rules.structure: Rarely + auxiliary + subject + main verb.
notes: Use do-support if there is no auxiliary.
The meaning is emphatic and formal.

rules.title: 2. As ... as comparatives
rules.explanation: Use as + adjective + as to show equality.
rules.structure: as + adjective + as + noun/pronoun.
notes: Use the subject pronoun form after as in formal writing.
Hers replaces her command of syntax.

common_mistakes.wrong: Rarely I have seen such dedication.
common_mistakes.correct: Rarely have I seen such dedication.
common_mistakes.reason: Rarely at the beginning requires inversion.

other_examples.sentence: Seldom have I read a more persuasive argument.
other_examples.translation: Jarang sekali saya membaca argumen yang lebih persuasif.

other_examples.sentence: Her analysis is as rigorous as his.
other_examples.translation: Analisisnya sama ketatnya dengan analisisnya.

multiErrorSegments.text: which set out in the appendix
correctAnswers: which are set out in the appendix

details_explanation.explanation: The relative clause which set out in the appendix is missing a passive verb. The correct form is which are set out or the reduced form set out. The mandative subjunctive be allocated is correct.
details_explanation.introduction: Relative clauses with a passive meaning need be + past participle unless the relative pronoun and auxiliary are reduced. The verb decide that can take the subjunctive.

rules.title: 1. Passive relative clauses
rules.explanation: Use which/that + be + past participle in a full passive relative clause.
rules.structure: noun + which + be + past participle.
notes: The reduced form omits which and be.
Set out is the past participle of set.

rules.title: 2. Subjunctive after decide
rules.explanation: Decide that can be followed by the base subjunctive in formal English.
rules.structure: decide + that + subject + base verb.
notes: Be allocated is passive subjunctive.
Should be allocated is an alternative.

common_mistakes.wrong: the criteria which set out in the appendix
common_mistakes.correct: the criteria which are set out in the appendix
common_mistakes.reason: The relative clause needs a passive verb.

other_examples.sentence: The rules, which are set out in the handbook, apply to everyone.
other_examples.translation: Aturan, yang tercantum dalam buku panduan, berlaku untuk semua orang.

other_examples.sentence: The board decided that the policy be reviewed.
other_examples.translation: Dewan memutuskan agar kebijakan itu ditinjau.

details_explanation.explanation: By the time the auditors arrived establishes a point in the past. The earlier action must be in the past perfect: had already shredded. The non-defining relative clause which was a serious offence is correct.
details_explanation.introduction: The past perfect is used for an action completed before another past action. By the time introduces the later event.

rules.title: 1. Past perfect with by the time
rules.explanation: Use had + past participle for the earlier action.
rules.structure: By the time + past simple, subject + had + past participle.
notes: The later event is in the past simple.
Already often appears with the past perfect.

rules.title: 2. Non-defining relative clauses
rules.explanation: Which can refer to a whole clause and is separated by a comma.
rules.structure: clause, which + verb ...
notes: Which was a serious offence refers to the whole preceding action.
That is not used in this way.

common_mistakes.wrong: By the time we arrived, the film already started.
common_mistakes.correct: By the time we arrived, the film had already started.
common_mistakes.reason: The earlier action requires the past perfect.

other_examples.sentence: By the time the police arrived, the thief had escaped.
other_examples.translation: Pada saat polisi tiba, pencuri sudah kabur.

other_examples.sentence: He failed the exam, which surprised no one.
other_examples.translation: Dia gagal ujian, yang tidak mengejutkan siapa pun.

details_explanation.explanation: The comparative correlative the more ... the more requires the comparative adjective before the subject and verb: the more determined he became. The structure the more he became determined is ungrammatical.
details_explanation.introduction: The more ... the more is a correlative construction showing parallel increase. The comparative phrase comes first in each clause.

rules.title: 1. Comparative correlative
rules.explanation: Use the + comparative at the beginning of each clause.
rules.structure: The + comparative + subject + verb, the + comparative + subject + verb.
notes: The comparative adjective stays before the subject.
Do not insert became before the adjective.

rules.title: 2. Adjective order with become
rules.explanation: Become is a linking verb followed by an adjective.
rules.structure: subject + become + adjective.
notes: The adjective describes the subject.
In the correlative, the adjective is fronted with more.

common_mistakes.wrong: The more he became tired, the more he made mistakes.
common_mistakes.correct: The more tired he became, the more mistakes he made.
common_mistakes.reason: The comparative adjective must be fronted in the correlative.

other_examples.sentence: The more carefully you listen, the more you will notice.
other_examples.translation: Semakin cermat Anda mendengarkan, semakin banyak yang Anda perhatikan.

other_examples.sentence: The longer the meeting lasted, the more impatient everyone became.
other_examples.translation: Semakin lama rapat berlangsung, semakin tidak sabar semua orang.

details_explanation.explanation: Should you require is an inverted first conditional. After should, the base form require is used, not the past form required. The formal request please do not hesitate to contact is correct.
details_explanation.introduction: Should + subject + base verb is a formal alternative to If + subject + present simple. It is common in business and legal writing.

rules.title: 1. Inverted should-conditional
rules.explanation: Omit if and place should before the subject.
rules.structure: Should + subject + base verb, subject + modal + verb.
notes: Use the base form after should.
The main clause often contains will, can or an imperative.

rules.title: 2. Formal requests
rules.explanation: Do not hesitate to + infinitive is a fixed polite formula.
rules.structure: Please do not hesitate to + base verb.
notes: The undersigned is a formal way to refer to the writer.
This register is common in letters and emails.

common_mistakes.wrong: Should you required anything, let me know.
common_mistakes.correct: Should you require anything, let me know.
common_mistakes.reason: The base form follows should.

other_examples.sentence: Should you have any questions, please contact our office.
other_examples.translation: Jika Anda memiliki pertanyaan, silakan hubungi kantor kami.

other_examples.sentence: Should the weather deteriorate, the event will be cancelled.
other_examples.translation: Jika cuaca memburuk, acara akan dibatalkan.

details_explanation.explanation: Only after at the beginning of a sentence triggers inversion in the main clause: did the authorities release. The passive past perfect had been concluded is correct.
details_explanation.introduction: Only after, only when and only then are restrictive adverbials that cause inversion in the main clause.

rules.title: 1. Inversion after only after
rules.explanation: The main clause uses auxiliary + subject + main verb.
rules.structure: Only after + clause, auxiliary + subject + main verb.
notes: The inversion is in the main clause, not the after-clause.
Use did with the past simple.

rules.title: 2. Past perfect passive
rules.explanation: The earlier action is had been + past participle.
rules.structure: subject + had been + past participle.
notes: The investigation had been concluded is passive.
The main clause then uses the past simple.

common_mistakes.wrong: Only after the meeting ended the decision was announced.
common_mistakes.correct: Only after the meeting ended was the decision announced.
common_mistakes.reason: Only after requires inversion in the main clause.

other_examples.sentence: Only after the evidence was examined did the jury reach a verdict.
other_examples.translation: Baru setelah bukti diperiksa, juri mencapai putusan.

other_examples.sentence: Only when the rain stopped did we leave the shelter.
other_examples.translation: Baru setelah hujan berhenti, kami meninggalkan tempat berlindung.

details_explanation.explanation: The cleft structure It was not until ... is completed by that, not when. The verb revealed is in the correct past simple because the cleft focuses on a past time.
details_explanation.introduction: It was not until + time + that + clause is an emphatic way to say something did not happen before a certain time.

rules.title: 1. Not until cleft
rules.explanation: Use that to introduce the clause after the focused time expression.
rules.structure: It was not until + time + that + subject + past simple.
notes: When is not used in this cleft.
The main verb is not inverted.

rules.title: 2. Tense in the cleft
rules.explanation: The verb in the that-clause matches the time of the narrative.
rules.structure: It was not until ... that + past simple.
notes: The focus is on the late time.
Do not use the past perfect unless the sequence requires it.

common_mistakes.wrong: It was not until midnight when he arrived.
common_mistakes.correct: It was not until midnight that he arrived.
common_mistakes.reason: The cleft is completed by that, not when.

other_examples.sentence: It was not until the war ended that the truth emerged.
other_examples.translation: Baru setelah perang berakhir, kebenaran terungkap.

other_examples.sentence: It was not until she left that he realized his mistake.
other_examples.translation: Baru setelah dia pergi, dia menyadari kesalahannya.

details_explanation.explanation: As much as introduces a concessive clause meaning although. It cannot be followed by but because the concession is already expressed. The correct clause is simply I cannot condone his methods.
details_explanation.introduction: Much as and as much as are concessive structures meaning although. They introduce a contrast without a second conjunction.

rules.title: 1. Concessive as much as
rules.explanation: As much as + clause expresses concession.
rules.structure: As much as + subject + verb, + main clause.
notes: The main clause is not introduced by but.
The structure is formal and emphatic.

rules.title: 2. No double conjunction
rules.explanation: A concessive subordinator cannot be paired with but.
rules.structure: Although/though/as much as + clause, + main clause.
notes: But is redundant after a concessive clause.
Yet can be used for emphasis in some styles, but not but.

common_mistakes.wrong: Although he was tired, but he continued.
common_mistakes.correct: Although he was tired, he continued.
common_mistakes.reason: Although and but are not used together.

other_examples.sentence: Much as I respect her, I cannot agree with her conclusion.
other_examples.translation: Meskipun saya menghormatinya, saya tidak bisa menyetujui kesimpulannya.

other_examples.sentence: As much as he wanted to stay, he had to leave.
other_examples.translation: Meskipun dia ingin tinggal, dia harus pergi.

details_explanation.explanation: The report was drafted, so the perfect participle must be passive: having been drafted. The reduced form drafted is also possible. The modal perfect passive could have been avoided is correct.
details_explanation.introduction: Perfect participles can be active (having written) or passive (having been written). The choice depends on whether the subject performs or receives the action.

rules.title: 1. Perfect passive participle
rules.explanation: Use having been + past participle when the subject receives the action.
rules.structure: Having been + past participle, + main clause.
notes: The active form having drafted would mean the report drafted something.
The reduced form drafted is also acceptable.

rules.title: 2. Modal perfect passive

It is common in academic writing.

rules.title: 2. Perfect infinitive passive
rules.explanation: Use to have been + past participle for an earlier passive action.
rules.structure: to have been + past participle.
notes: To have written would mean the manuscript wrote something.
The twelfth century is earlier than the discovery.

common_mistakes.wrong: The temple is believed to have built in 500 BC.
common_mistakes.correct: The temple is believed to have been built in 500 BC.

details_explanation.explanation: After would rather ... than, the infinitive is used without to: than attend. The perfect form have stayed is correct for a past preference.
details_explanation.introduction: Would rather + bare infinitive is followed by than + bare infinitive. The two infinitives should be parallel.

rules.title: 1. Would rather ... than
rules.explanation: Use the bare infinitive after than.
rules.structure: would rather + bare infinitive + than + bare infinitive.
notes: To is not used after than.
The structure expresses preference.

rules.title: 2. Perfect infinitive
rules.explanation: Would rather have + past participle refers to the past.
rules.structure: would rather have + past participle + than + bare infinitive.
notes: Have stayed is the perfect infinitive.
The second infinitive remains bare.

common_mistakes.wrong: I would rather stay than to go out.
common_mistakes.correct: I would rather stay than go out.
common_mistakes.reason: The bare infinitive follows than.

other_examples.sentence: She would rather resign than compromise her principles.

other_examples.sentence: They would rather have cancelled the event than postpone it.
other_examples.translation: Mereka lebih suka membatalkan acara itu daripada menundanya.

details_explanation.explanation: After provided that, the present simple is used to refer to the future: the conditions are met. The main clause will be signed correctly uses will.
details_explanation.introduction: Provided that, on condition that and as long as introduce conditions. The condition clause uses the present simple for future meaning.

rules.title: 1. Tense in conditional clauses
rules.explanation: Do not use will in the condition clause.
rules.structure: Provided that + present simple, + will + base verb.
notes: Are met is present simple passive.
Will is used only in the main clause.

rules.title: 2. Passive present simple
rules.explanation: The passive present simple is am/is/are + past participle.
rules.structure: subject + are + past participle.
notes: The conditions are met is passive.
The main clause is also passive.

common_mistakes.wrong: Provided that it will rain, the match will be cancelled.
common_mistakes.correct: Provided that it rains, the match will be cancelled.
common_mistakes.reason: The condition clause uses the present simple.

details_explanation.explanation: The clause how little one knows is an embedded question, so it uses statement word order, not inversion. The comparative correlative the more ... the more is correct.
details_explanation.introduction: Embedded questions and nominal clauses use statement word order: subject + verb. Inversion occurs only in direct questions.

rules.title: 1. Embedded question word order
rules.explanation: Do not invert after how, what, where, whether, etc. in an embedded clause.
rules.structure: how + adjective/adverb + subject + verb.
notes: How little one knows is correct.
Does is not used.

rules.title: 2. Comparative correlative
rules.explanation: The more ... the more shows parallel increase.
rules.structure: The more + subject + verb, the more + subject + verb.
notes: Both clauses use statement word order.
The structure is not inverted.

common_mistakes.wrong: I wonder where does he live.
common_mistakes.correct: I wonder where he lives.
common_mistakes.reason: Embedded questions do not invert.

other_examples.sentence: The more she practiced, the more confident she became.

details_explanation.explanation: Essential that requires the mandative subjunctive, and the passive subjunctive is be interviewed. The present indicative is interviewed is not used in this formal structure.
details_explanation.introduction: Adjectives such as essential, vital and imperative trigger the base subjunctive in a following that-clause.

rules.title: 1. Subjunctive after essential
rules.explanation: Use the base form of the verb in the that-clause.
rules.structure: It is essential + that + subject + base verb.
notes: Be interviewed is passive subjunctive.
Should be interviewed is an alternative.

rules.title: 2. Passive subjunctive
rules.explanation: The passive subjunctive is be + past participle.
rules.structure: that + subject + be + past participle.
notes: Be is invariable.
The agent is introduced by by.

common_mistakes.wrong: It is essential that the sample is stored correctly.
common_mistakes.correct: It is essential that the sample be stored correctly.
common_mistakes.reason: Essential that takes the base subjunctive.

other_examples.sentence: It is vital that all safety checks be completed before departure.

other_examples.sentence: It is imperative that the data be backed up daily.

details_explanation.explanation: By no means is a negative adverbial and requires inversion: should this information be disclosed. The passive modal should be + past participle is correct after inversion.
details_explanation.introduction: By no means, in no way and under no circumstances are negative adverbials that trigger inversion of the modal and subject.

rules.title: 1. Negative inversion
rules.explanation: Place the modal before the subject.
rules.structure: Negative adverbial + modal + subject + main verb.
notes: The main verb remains in the base form.
The structure is formal and emphatic.

rules.title: 2. Passive with should
rules.explanation: The passive is should be + past participle.
rules.structure: should + subject + be + past participle.
notes: Be disclosed is correct.
Do not use should be disclosing.

common_mistakes.wrong: By no means this should be allowed.
common_mistakes.correct: By no means should this be allowed.
common_mistakes.reason: By no means requires inversion.

other_examples.sentence: By no means is the result conclusive.

other_examples.sentence: Under no circumstances should these files be removed.

details_explanation.explanation: The findings are disproven by others, so the passive infinitive is required: have yet to be disproven. The concessive though controversial is correct.
details_explanation.introduction: Have yet to + infinitive means have not yet + past participle. The infinitive is passive when the subject receives the action.

rules.title: 1. Have yet to + infinitive
rules.explanation: This formal structure means something has not happened yet.
rules.structure: subject + have/has yet to + base verb.
notes: The meaning is negative.
It is common in formal writing.

rules.title: 2. Passive infinitive
rules.explanation: Use to be + past participle when the subject receives the action.
rules.structure: to be + past participle.
notes: To be disproven is passive.
The agent is introduced by by.

common_mistakes.wrong: The theory has yet to prove.
common_mistakes.correct: The theory has yet to be proven.
common_mistakes.reason: The theory receives the action, so the passive infinitive is needed.

other_examples.sentence: The proposal, though promising, has yet to be approved.

details_explanation.explanation: The inverted third conditional requires the past participle sounded, not the base form sound. The main clause would have spread is correct.
details_explanation.introduction: In negative inverted conditionals, not comes after the subject: Had + subject + not + past participle.

rules.title: 1. Negative inversion
rules.explanation: Place not after the subject in an inverted conditional.
rules.structure: Had + subject + not + past participle, subject + would have + past participle.
notes: Sound is the base form and is incorrect.
Sounded is the past participle.

rules.title: 2. Conditional perfect
rules.explanation: The result uses would have + past participle.
rules.structure: subject + would have + past participle.
notes: Would have spread is correct.
The time reference is past.

common_mistakes.wrong: Had he not arrive, we would have left.
common_mistakes.correct: Had he not arrived, we would have left.
common_mistakes.reason: The past participle is required after had.

details_explanation.explanation: Having deliberated for hours must refer to the subject of the main clause. A verdict cannot deliberate, so the main clause must be active with the committee or jury as subject.
details_explanation.introduction: Perfect participle clauses describe an action completed before the main action. Their understood subject must match the main subject.

rules.title: 1. Dangling perfect participle
rules.explanation: Rewrite the main clause so that its subject performs the participle action.
rules.structure: Having + past participle, + subject (same doer) + verb.
notes: The committee or jury deliberates.
The verdict is the result, not the doer.

rules.title: 2. Active vs passive main clause
rules.explanation: Choose active voice when the subject performs the action.
rules.structure: subject + past simple + object.
notes: Reached a verdict is active.
Was reached is passive and creates a dangling modifier.

common_mistakes.wrong: Having examined the evidence, a decision was reached.
common_mistakes.correct: Having examined the evidence, the panel reached a decision.
common_mistakes.reason: The panel, not the decision, examined the evidence.

details_explanation.explanation: Under no circumstances requires inversion: are employees permitted. The passive are permitted + to-infinitive is correct.
details_explanation.introduction: Negative adverbials at the beginning of a clause cause inversion of the auxiliary and subject.

rules.title: 1. Inversion with be
rules.explanation: Place the form of be before the subject.
rules.structure: Negative adverbial + be + subject + past participle.
notes: Are employees permitted is correct.
The passive infinitive follows.

rules.title: 2. Passive + to-infinitive
rules.explanation: Permit takes a to-infinitive in the passive.
rules.structure: be permitted + to + base verb.
notes: To remove is correct.
The agent is not expressed.

common_mistakes.wrong: Under no circumstances visitors are allowed entry.
common_mistakes.correct: Under no circumstances are visitors allowed entry.
common_mistakes.reason: The negative adverbial requires inversion.

details_explanation.explanation: The sentence combines an it-cleft, a concessive phrase and the mandative subjunctive. Insist that requires be put, not is put.
details_explanation.introduction: It-clefts emphasize a noun phrase. Concessive phrases with despite introduce contrast. Insist that takes the base subjunctive.

rules.title: 1. It-cleft with who
rules.explanation: Use it was + noun + who + clause to focus on a person.
rules.structure: It was + noun phrase + who + verb.
notes: The chairman is the focus.
Who refers to the chairman.

rules.title: 2. Subjunctive after insist
rules.explanation: Use the base form be in the passive subjunctive.
rules.structure: insist + that + subject + be + past participle.
notes: Be put is correct.
Is put is indicative and not used here.

common_mistakes.wrong: He insisted that the vote is taken.
common_mistakes.correct: He insisted that the vote be taken.
common_mistakes.reason: Insist that takes the base subjunctive.

multiErrorSegments.text: she had read the letter twice

details_explanation.explanation: Not until at the beginning triggers inversion in the main clause: did she understand. The past perfect had read is correct for the earlier action.
details_explanation.introduction: Not until + clause + auxiliary + subject + main verb is an emphatic negative structure meaning she did not understand until she had read the letter twice.

rules.title: 1. Inversion after not until
rules.explanation: The main clause uses auxiliary + subject + base verb.
rules.structure: Not until + clause, did + subject + base verb.
notes: Understood becomes understand after did.
The until-clause is not inverted.

rules.title: 2. Past perfect
rules.explanation: The action in the until-clause happened before the main action.
rules.structure: had + past participle.
notes: Had read is correct.
The main clause then uses the past simple after did.

common_mistakes.wrong: Not until he left she realized the truth.
common_mistakes.correct: Not until he left did she realize the truth.
common_mistakes.reason: Not until requires inversion in the main clause.
